tier_reason: bench/README.md publishes both snapshots against evmone v0.23.0 (baseline and advanced) and revm 43.0.2 from public harness code (bench/src/compare.zig, bench/evmone/vm_loop.cpp, bench/revm/src/main.rs, fixtures under bench/fixtures/vm-loop), with the exact command line, ReleaseFast and frame-pointer flags in bench/build.zig, Zig 0.16 toolchain (bench/build.zig.zon minimum_zig_version 0.16.0) and a named CPU (Apple M1 Max). Every number in claimed_speedup matches the page.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig >= 0.16.0 (bench/build.zig.zon), zig build bench-compare -Dbench-optimize=ReleaseFast -Dbench-support-min=osaka -Dbench-support-max=osaka -Dnative-keccak=xkcp -- --spec osaka --num-runs 100 --warmup-ms 100 (five repeats, median of the five per-run medians); evmz modules built with omit_frame_pointer; evmone v0.23.0 with intx 0.15.0 compiled inside the Zig build by Zig's bundled clang from a hand-listed source set with -std=c++20 -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (not evmone's own CMake Release build); revm =43.0.2 built with cargo --release, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=no, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CODEGEN_UNITS=1 (Rust toolchain version not pinned for the sidecar).
corrections.caveats: Comparison is VM-core only: interpreter execute() with analysis prepared outside the timed window, no transaction validation, journal or database, so it is not a whole-client comparison (the repo says the executor lane is deliberately later). Correctness check in all three runners is limited to a success status (evmz result status, evmone EVMC_SUCCESS in bench/evmone/vm_loop.cpp, revm InterpreterAction::Return with is_ok() in bench/revm/src/main.rs); bench/src/compare.zig only collects timings and host call counts and does not assert that return data, gas used or logs match across engines. The README headline table shows the four rows where evmz wins; the full M1 table also has rows where evmone-baseline is faster (MSTORE loop 0.67x, LOG0 0-byte 0.69x, LOG0 32-byte 0.58x, LOG4 0-byte 0.80x, ten-thousand-hashes 0.86x), and on the AMD snapshot evmz is within about 7% of evmone-base on 9 of 14 rows (ratios 0.94x to 1.07x, derived from page data) and slower on the LOG0 rows (0.73x, 0.75x). The AMD snapshot is older, run in a KVM guest pinned to one CPU, and names only the EPYC Genoa family, not a model. The M1 snapshot enables evmz's optional XKCP Keccak provider while evmone uses its bundled keccak.c, so the keccak-heavy rows partly compare hash implementations. The evmone baseline is compiled by Zig's clang from a hand-picked source list and flag set rather than evmone's CMake Release build, and revm's sidecar has no pinned Rust version. Revm is timed through its raw interpreter (Interpreter::run_plain), not a transaction path. The project is pre-release (version 0.0.0, unaudited) and contains CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted development); first-party numbers only, 3 stars. Not the cryptuon/zig-evm project, which is rejected for a hard-coded table.

notes: All M1 and AMD figures and ratios in the record match bench/README.md and the README Performance table; harness, flags and versions confirmed in bench/build.zig and bench/build.zig.zon (evmone v0.23.0, intx v0.15.0, revm =43.0.2). Shortcomings to record: VM-core-only scope, status-only correctness checks with no cross-engine output or gas comparison, evmone-base faster on 5 of 14 M1 rows and near parity on the older AMD run, evmone built outside its CMake build, XKCP Keccak only on the evmz side, first-party with 3 stars. Last commit 2026-10-05 (Native contract #73), MIT OR Apache-2.0, not a fork.

tier_reason: Independent individual's gist (not by hxcpp's developers) timing the public HashLink other/benchs suite, whose upstream runner (other/benchs/Benchs.hx) checks every program's result and subtracts startup; CPU models (Intel Core i5-6600, AMD Ryzen 7 7700) are stated but Haxe/hxcpp versions, the C++ compiler and its flags are not, and the gist's extended runner (cs, java, lua, php, python targets) is not published, so it falls short of A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the gist. The upstream HashLink runner (other/benchs/Benchs.hx) compiles each benchmark with haxe -cpp cpp -main <name> -dce full -D HXCPP_SILENT -D HXCPP_GC_GENERATIONAL and leaves C++ compilation to hxcpp's default toolchain; the gist's own runner, which adds cs, java, lua, php and python targets, is not included in the gist, so its flags are unconfirmed.
corrections.workload: tong's gist 'Haxe benchmarks' (one results file, three revisions, last active 2025-09-20) running the HashLink repository's other/benchs suite (Startup, Anonymous, BinaryTrees, Fib, FloatArray, IntArray, Mandelbrot, NBodies) compiled from the same Haxe source to each target (js, cpp, cs, hl, java, lua, neko, php, python; hlc and jvm in the 2025 rerun). In the upstream runner each program is re-launched until 1 s of total time accumulates (first run discarded), the output is checked against the expected @:result value, the per-target Startup time is subtracted, and the mean is truncated to 0.01 s. 2018 run plus a September 2025 rerun in a comment.
corrections.caveats: The measurements are an individual's gist, not an official suite, and neither Haxe nor hxcpp versions, the C++ compiler or its flags are given, so the run is below tier A (the benchmark sources are public in HaxeFoundation/hashlink other/benchs, but the gist holds only results and its runner was extended beyond the upstream hl/hlc/js/neko/cpp target list). The suite comes from the HashLink repository, i.e. from the baseline's own project. The 2025 rerun lists no totals and shows hlc (HashLink's own C output) failing the result check on every benchmark ('result 0 but expected ...') and lua erroring on BinaryTrees, so hxcpp is never compared with HashLink/C, the AOT path closest to it. Even against HashLink the win is not on every row: HL/JIT beat cpp on Anonymous in 2018 (0.29 s versus 0.38 s). Against the other baselines the win is not clear: in 2018 JavaScript beat cpp on Anonymous (0.02 versus 0.38) and Java on BinaryTrees and Mandelbrot (0.06 versus 0.08, 0.12 versus 0.13), the totals put C++ 0.72 s next to Java 0.81 and JavaScript 0.96, and in the 2025 rows JVM and Node are faster than cpp on several rows (Anonymous 0.03 and 0.02 versus 0.1, BinaryTrees 0.02 versus 0.05, Mandelbrot 0.07 versus 0.13; derived from page data). Times are truncated to 0.01 s after startup subtraction, so many cells are 0 or 0.01 and small ratios are unreliable. The official HaxeBenchmarks site benchs.haxe.org exists but was blocked (EGRESS_BLOCKED), and its GitHub repo HaxeBenchmarks/benchs.haxe.org holds the site code, not result data. hxcpp is an AOT C++ backend and runtime rather than a VM, so the comparison is AOT against interpreters and JITs. The hxcpp LICENSE.txt is a one-condition BSD notice (BSD-1-Clause) that adds 'See individual source files for additional license information', so bundled third-party code carries its own terms.

notes: Gist numbers verified: 2018 runtimes and totals (cpp 0.7166 s, java 0.806, js 0.962, hl 5.678, neko 27.16, so about 7.9x over HashLink and 38x over Neko, derived from page data) and every 2025 cpp/hl/neko value match the record. Tier B kept on the independent-measurement rule; if the orchestrator reads B strictly as peer-reviewed or well-known suite, this is C. Shortcomings: no compiler or flags, runner not published in the gist, hlc never compared, JVM/Node match or beat cpp on several rows, 0.01 s truncation. Last commit 2026-09-22, 329 stars, BSD-1-Clause.

tier_reason: The README carries only first-party throughput and cost claims (over 1 million Merkleized TPS, near-linear scaling to 96 cores, 91% cheaper than unnamed sharded execution) from LayerZero Labs' own preprint; bench-sendeth code is public but no hardware, no baseline run (sequential revm, pevm or Block-STM) and no result table are in the repo, and the paper was unreachable.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.85.0 (rust-toolchain.toml); benchmark run with cargo run --release through bench-sendeth/run.sh (which exports RUSTFLAGS=-Awarnings); release profile opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units 16, panic=abort; revm 20.0.0 and alloy 0.11.1 per workspace Cargo.toml. Paper reproduction commands: run.sh --size full with --generator none, hotn (--contention-degree 0.1 --skew 100) or replay.
corrections.caveats: Not a faster-than-baseline claim in the sense of the listed baselines: neither the README nor bench-sendeth compares against sequential revm or pevm on a common workload (the only comparison in the README is '91% cheaper than sharded execution', a cost figure against an unnamed baseline, with the methodology in LayerZero Labs' own paper, which is blocked here: layerzero.network, arxiv.org and emergentmind.com returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the paper's numbers come from search-result text only). The workloads are plain ETH and ERC-20 transfers, which is far easier to parallelise than general contract code; the paper is 'Under submission' (not peer reviewed) and is written by the vendor. The repo holds a single 'Initial commit' dated 2025-06-26, so there is no development history to check, and the 96-vCPU machine is only known from a third-party article snippet. bench-sendeth writes a metrics JSON per run but no published result file is in the repo. FAFO is a transaction scheduler and parallel execution pipeline on revm plus QMDB, not a bytecode VM, so the bytecode-vms-and-wasm filing is a loose fit. pevm and revm are catalogued separately, and Block-STM style comparison, if any, is in the unopened paper.

notes: README claims match the record; repo is one 'Initial commit' (2025-06-26), 65 stars, 13 forks, MIT and Apache-2.0, not a fork; stale is correct (15 months). Shortcomings to record: no baseline timing in repo (only a cost ratio vs unnamed sharded execution), vendor preprint not peer reviewed and unreachable, transfer-only workloads, no hardware in repo, weak category fit (scheduler, not VM).
